Bill (No. 106) to incorporate the Lake-Erie and Northern Railway Company.- Mr. Harris.

Mr. CONMEE moved for leave to introduce a Bill to amend chapter 139, 4 and 5,. Edward VII., intituled an Act respecting the Ontario and Minnesota Power Company, Ltd. He said: The object of the Bill is^ to amend the Act of 1905, chapter 139, relating to the Rainy river at Fort Francis, which is a navigable river, and also an international stream; hence the necessity of federal legislation dealing with it. Works have been carried out upon the river which interfere with the navigation of the stream, and which have changed the conditions in connection with the Canadian canal that was constructed some years ago at that point. They also interfere with the water necessary for the navigation of the river, not only below the works, but also of Rainy lake, situated above the works. The question is considerably involved. It will be necessary, as I consider, to give some of the history of the conditions and circumstances leading up to the present situation to do That would involve a reference to agreements, to Acts of the provincial legislature, and to Acts of the federal parliament of Canada. These works were proceeded with a good deal in the manner in which such works are ordinarily undertaken. The first permission, as far as the federal authorities are concerned, to go on with the works was obtained by an order in council on the submission and approval of plans. The works have not been carried on according to those plans, but quite different plans have been adopted. After the works were constructed the company desired to have the changed plans ratified, but they have not been ratified by the Minister of Public Works of the Dominion, and, therefore, the work stands in that position. Hence the importance of making some regulation by enactment by which the public interest in the navigable stream and the chain of navigation both above and below should be dealt with. I assume that the Bill *would have to go to a committee. Although it is a public Bill, I think the practice has been, where there are questions which might affect the private interests of individuals, or of a company, to refer it to a committee of the House. I may say that it is not the intention of the amendment to take away from that company any rights they now have under existing legislation, or to impose upon them new or more onerous conditions. The object is to clear awav doubts that have arisen and to enact such legislation as will enable the proper protection of the public interest in the

matters involved. As it would take me a Ions time to go through these various documents with the necessity, here and there of short explanations of what has led ud to the present condition, I would ask, instead of taking up the time of the House for some considerable time, as the question is involved and I take it that the Bill will get its first reading and be referred to the Private Bills, or th'e Railway Committee, that, in the meantime, I be permitted to put this record on ' Hansard.' Hon. members will then have before them the information which is necessary to an intelligent understanding of the question. When the Bill comes up, either in committee or in this House, for its second reading, or in Committee of the Whole House, hon. members will be able to discuss it very much more to advantage than can be done to-day under the circumstances. If I am permitted to hand these papers to ' Hansard ' and allow the Bill to go through its first reading I will not take up any more of the time of the House.
I am unable to give permission as far as ' Hansard ' is concerned.
I do not quite understand you, Mr. Speaker.
I understand that only tables of figures are allowed to be put in ' Hansard,' and that nothing else can be put in ' Hansard ' unless it is spoken in the House.

Then I shall have to make reference to these various documents. I may say that the development of this power, which affects the public interest in the manner I have shortly outlined was entered into as a joint undertaking, an international work, upon the strength of an agreement that was entered into at the request of the town of Fort Francis, and, on their behalf, by the government of Ontario, in 1904. I conceive it to be necessary to make reference to the agreement, as it is the foundation of the whole transaction, and, perhaps, I may be permitted, instead of reading this document, which is somewhat lengthy, to hand it in to ' Hansard.'

Well, unfortunately, I feel bound, then, under these circumstances, to read the document:-
Memorandum of agreement made in triplicate . this 17th day of February, 1901, between His Majesty represented by the Hon. the Commissioner of Crown Lands of the province of Ontario, hereinafter called the government.

Could not my hon. friend use this document to the same advantage
before the committee? I do not wish to interfere with my hon. friend, because this is his right, but I was only making that suggestion, and it will likely have to be gone over again when the committee meets to discuss the Bill. I cannot just see how the reading will help the hon. gentleman in his case.

I feel disposed to accept that suggestion if I understand it aright. I understand the hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) to suggest that instead of going into this matter in detail to-day, the Bill be read the first time, and that this information be used before the committee to which it may be referred.

I was expressing my individual opinion of it. I suppose that the question as to whether the Bill should be read a first time is a matter for the House to deal with. I was only directing my attention to the very large volume of records which the hon. gentleman has and suggesting that they might be presented to the committee which deals with the Bill.

I think that if my hon. friend would do that it would result in better economy of the time of the House. It has been the practice in this House to have very little discussion upon the first reading and especially not to introduce documents or the like of that. It all has to be gone over again on the second reading, and it duplicates time and expense. I think the Speaker has been very generally in accord with that idea, and has always suggested that the first reading be limited to a mere explanation of the Bill without the introduction of arguments.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Every Bill presented to this House is accepted for the first reading as a matter of course unless there is on the face of the Bill a paramount objection. There can be no objection to the Bill of my hon. friend being introduced; but, if I am correctly informed, he is attempting to amend a private Act, and there is a regular procedure to be followed in such a case. If it is a public Bill, there is no objection at all to the first reading.

The Bill is to amend a private Act, but it deals with a'public question. The whole object of chapter 139 of 4 and 5 Edward VII. is to regulate certain works and the public rights in regard to those works. The Interpretation Act provides that all Bills, whether private or otherwise, are considered public Bills. Section 18 of that Act reads in this way:
Every Act shall be so construed as to reserve to parliament the power of repealing or amending it, and of revoking, restricting or modifying any power, privilege or advantage thereby vested in or granted to any per-

son, whenever such repeal, amendment, revocation, restriction or modification is deemed by parliament to be required for the public good.
I do not wish to take up the time of the House, and if the Bill can be read the first time and be sent to the committee, I am quite willing to accept that situation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: So far as I have been able to follow my hon. friend, he is attempting to amend a private Act, and in that case there are certain rules which have to be followed. The parties concerned may desire to be heard. It is for the Speaker to decide whether the Bill is in order or not in order, and I would suggest to my hon. friend that he present his case so as to obtain the ruling of the Speaker on that point.

I think my hon. friend should address himself to the point just mentioned. It seems to be absolutely impossible that any gentleman, desiring that a private Act shall be amended, can get rid of all the requirements of this House with respect to notice and advertisement by introducing his proposed amendment as a public Bill.

I am quite willing to discuss that point if it is necessary^ to raise it at this time; but I did not think that would be necessary. This is not the first public Bill that has amended a private Act. I submit that the practice of parliament and the authorities sustain the position I take. I find the following in Bouri-not, at page 688:
As a rule it may be stated that when Bills treat of matters of general policy, such as sanitary, or police, or commercial, or fiscal regnlations, they may be considered as public measures. In fact, all Bills affecting the general interests of the community and involving considerations of public policy, are out of the category of Private Bills dealing with the special interests of corporations or associations.
I submit that this is a Bill of that character, not dealing with the private interests of anybody, hut with matters of public interest and public policy. Further on Bouri-not says:
Whenever public Bills involve private interests, which should be carefully guarded they are subjected to the same examination provided for private Bills.
He goes on to show that such Bills are referred to the committee. I find that several Bills of that character have passed the parliament of Canada, and I have no objection to this Bill going to the committee. Perhaps this case, referred to by Bourinot, might be cited as fully warranting the course I am taking:

In' the session of 1875, the Premier (Mr. Mackenzie) moved for leave to introduce a public Bill to rearrange the ' capital of the Noitliern Railway of Canada, to enable the said company to change the gauge of its railway, and to provide for the release of the government lien on the road on certain conditions.' Objection having been taken that seme of the provisions affected private interests and altered the powers of the company in very material points^ the Speaker decided that the Bill ought to be withdrawn. Separate Bills were subsequently passed by the House-one relating to the government lien, was treated as a public Bill, and the other, relating to the gauge and capital, as a private Bill.
This Bill may require treatment of that kind. If anything in it required to be cut out as not being within the legitimate scope of a public Bill, that could be done by the committee. According to Bourinot, all local and private Acts passed in Canada previous to and fox some years after 1840 contained a clause declaring that it should be deemed a public Act and should be judiciously taken notice of as such by the judges, justices of the peace, and other people, without being specially pleaded. From 1850 to 1860 the clause was shortened and it was simply enacted that it shall be deemed a public Act. Bourinot says further, that in the first session of the Dominion parliament it was enacted that every Act shall, except by express provision it is declared a private Act, be deemed a public Act and shall be judicially noted; and he says that consequently the public clause has been ever since omitted. The law and practice seems to be that unless there is a declaration in a private Act that it is such, then ever since confederation it is held to be a public measure. Under these circumstances, I would submit that this Bill might very well go to the committee, where it can be looked into, and if it is found to contain provisions that ought not be in a public Bill of this character, why of course the Bill can be dropped. I will be glad to have your ruling, Mr. Speaker, as to whether the Bill can be permitted to be introduced or not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is no doubt that my hon. friend is attempting to amend a private Act, and he may be right in his contention that it is possible to amend a private Act by a public Act, and to dispense with the notices, advertisements, &c. But, of course it is impossible for Mr. Speaker or the House to know whether this private Act can be amended by a public Act unless the hon. gentleman places his Bill before us. He will therefore, I think, be serving hik own case if he told us what is the nature/ and object of his Bill.

I desired before taking up the amending Bill to give the House information as to the circumstances and conditions which make this amendment necessary, if the public interest is to be protected. There was a joint arrangement for the development of the power by a dam from side to side of the Rainy river at Fort Frances, which is an international stream, and the works were commenced by order in council.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: A joint arrangement between whom?

A joint bargain between Mr. Backus, of Minneapolis, and the corporation of the town of Fort Frances, which was under an agreement bearing date 17th February, 1904, made at their request by the provincial government. I regret to have to take up the time of the House, but I feel it necessary in the public interest that I should do so. The community of Fort Frances have in my opinion and in their opinion been placed in a very unfortunate position. Rights which they had as natural rights, rights which they had by contract, rights which are vital to their future prosperity are attempted to be taken from them, and to deprive them of the use of the water power at the present time, and not only of the utilization of the power from this joint development but also of the navigation of the river. Several lines of steamers ply on that stream across the Lake of the Woods, and in a stretch of 100 miles of navigation on the river there are what is known as the Long Sault rapids, over which vessels cannot be navigated in low water. The goods are transferred from below the rapids to above the rapids and the people living along the stream are accommodated in that way. On two occasions since these works were erected that traffic has been cut off. in one case for nearly ten days. A vessel could not navigate the river for the reason that the gates were shut down and while the water was rising in the Rainy lake there was no navigation at all below the works. The same thing occurred on another occasion but not for the same length of time. At Fort Frances there is a lock which was built by this government many years ago at considerable cost. That lock is not now in operation. Goods are brought below the falls and transferred to vessels above the falls and carried on up to Rainy lake. That traffic has been entirely checked for weeks at a time because of the lack of construction^ of slides although such construction was imposed upon this company by the order in council authorizing it to go on with the work, and bv statute of this parliament, chap. 139. Still there is no redress. What Fort Frances is asking 90
for is not that the privileges which the company enjoys be taken away, but that the conditions under which the company obtained its franchise, the obligations that were placed upon it by order in council, and the plans which tihe company submitted, be complied with. I have referred to the plans. It was my intention to bring them here and lay them on the table, but I have not got them at present. I shall however, lay them on the table later so that hon. gentlemen may see that the first plan showed an equal number of units of water to be vented on each side of the International boundary, assuming that boundary to be in the centre of the stream. Hon. gentlemen will likewise see by the second plan that there is not an equal number of units on each side, but that there are more on the American than on the Canadian side. They will see by the first plan that this lock, which was previously constructed, was to have a gate at its upper entrance so that at any time the public could use the lock for navigation without difficulty. But what happened ? As will be seen by the second plan, which the minister refused to approve, the whole entrance to the lock has been blasted away. There have been three or four inlets made into it, the south wall of the lock has been entirely blasted away, and possession taken of that public property in such a way as to make it very expensive indeed to open it for navigation. I am not going to argue that it is not in the power of the government to force this company to remove the works I speak of, but what I do say is, that these people have gone on in a high handed manner, without authority and constructed works designed for the very purpose of forestalling the. operation of that canal. They planned their works, they planned their power-house in such a way that it is evident to any one -and I am sure the engineers of the department must know it-that these works were planned deliberately for the very purpose of forestalling the use either of the canal or the power on the Canadian side. The agreement to which I refer, provided that there should be a power-house on each side of the international line and the development of an equal quantity of power- one half the flow of the stream to be delivered on the Canadian side for use in Canada. The Act which was passed in 1905 by this parliament contains the same principle because it provides that the power shall be used concurrently on both sides and that there shall not be more power available for use on the American than on the Canadian side at any time. Now, if good faith had been kept, the conditions which.exist today at that point could not exist. What are these conditions? To-dav there is 18,000 horse-nower from that development being used for the purpose of operating pulp wood



grinder for the manufacture of paper on the American side, while there is not a single horse-power used on the Canadian side for any industrial purpose. I submit that that is not a concurrent development or use of the power such as parliament intended. I do not believe that .parliament ever intended to give this company the right to permanently take a greater portion of the power to the American side than the half to which they are entitled. I am aware that under Sec. 16-1 refer to the electrical exportation Act-there is power given to the Governor in Council to impose conditions and regulations and to stipulate not only with regard to the quantity of power that may be taken away for use in a foreign country but with regard to the power that shall be reserved for use in Canada. But I want to point out that that Act was passed three years aftel the agreement to which I have referred was entered into. I do not think it was the intention of parliament, in passing that Act to make it retroactive or take away the contractual rights of persons who had such rights previous to 1907. I refer to the order in council upon which this company got the right to proceed with its work, and 1 must say that this order in council is a very -extraordinary document. It compels me to make a little further explanation. In 1905 when .the company applied for incorpora-.tion to this parliament, the Bill that was introduced as Bill (No. 86); and if I may be permitted, I wish to read the Bill as introduced toy the company, for I think that is necessary to a proper understanding of the present position:-
Whereas, the Ontario and Minnesota Power Company, Limited, has by its petition represented that it was incorporated by letters patent under the general seal of the province of Ontario, dated 13th January, 1905, under the Ontario Companies Act, being chapter 191 of the revised statutes of Ontario, 1897.
Whereas the said company has prayed that it he enacted as hereinafter set forth and it is expedient to grant the prayers of the said petition, therefore His Majesty by the authority and advice of the Senate and Honse of Commons of Canada enacts as follows:-
The works of the Ontario and Minnesota Power Company, Limited, hereinafter called the company, are declared to he for the general advantage of Canada.
Section 2 refers to the capital stock of the company. The head office of the company is located in the city of Toronto.. The provisional directors are to be the gentlemen named in section 4, as follow:
4. The provisional directors of the company shall he Edward Wellington Backus, of the city of Minneapolis, in the state of Minnesota, one of the United States, Robert Alexander Grant, and Alexander McKenzie, of the city of Toronto, and William Johnston and Thomas Bremner Rankin, of the city of Ottawa, in the province of Ontario.

This has reference to chapter 139 *

referring to the production of power or
electrical energy, the delivery thereof, the construction of power-houses, &c.
So -that, while I do not wish to weary the House with too long quotations from this document it will be seen that [permission to go on with the work was granted subject to certain conditions.
That the permission he granted subject to the conditions inserted in the agreement between the government of the province of Ontario and the applicants and also subject to all the conditions and reservations expressed in the Act of parliament passed at its last session respecting the Ontario and Minnesota Power Company, Limited.
That no work will be done under the permission to he given to the company which will in any way interfere with the lock, canal, or other works of a public nature already executed at Fort Frances by the government of Canada, nor will any bridge of any other erection or construction of any nature whatsoever on, over or across the said lock, canal, or other works, be built, nor generally shall any use he made thereof except by permission in writing to that effect by the Minister of Public Works.
Now, I submit that this work has gone on quite irrespective of this provision. No such permission for the works to be erected has ever been obtained, and I have already pointed out the very damaging nature of the work. The reason for the application for this public Bill on behalf of Fort Frances may be given in this way. First, the town obtained an agreement to which they consented, and which was made on their behalf. Perhaps I may be permitted just to read the preamble of the agreement in order to show that my statement is fully borne out by the document itself.
Whereas the Rainy river is the district of Rainy river forms an International boundary between the province of Ontario in the Dominion of Canada and the state of Minnesota, one of the United States of America, which said river in the neighbourhood of the town of Fort Frances forms a valuable and extensive water-power;
And whereas the municipal council of the town of Fort Frances and the municipal council of the township of Mclrvine and the residents of the said town and township have at various times petitioned the government to develop or procure the development of the said water-power, so that the same might be utilized for municipal purposes and for manufacturing and milling in the said municipalities thereby assisting in the development of the said municipalities and of the surrounding districts;
And whereas application has been made by the purchasers for a grant in fee of such lands adjacent to the said river, and of such lands covered by the said river, and of such privileges as are necessary to enable the purchasers to develop the said water-power, and to render the same available for municipal marnfactnring and milling purposes;
.And whereas the sa'id water-power can he more advantageously developed, and more
power produced, jjy works embracing the entire width of the river, and dealing with it as a whole, than by an independent development on the Canadian side of the International boundary, and it is therefore in the public interest to adopt such plans of development;
And whereas the purchasers are the owners in fee simple of the lands and water-power on the Minnesota side of the International boundary opposite the said town of Fort Frances, and are desirous of obtaining from the government of the province of Ontario a grant in fee of the lands and power on the Canadian side of the International boundary, for the purpose of developing the water-power to the full capacity of the stream from side to side at high water mark, and of utilizing such storage facilities as may he available for maintaining the river at such high water mark, thereby rendering available a_large amount of power on the Canadian side of the river, for municipal purposes and for the operation of pulp and paper mills, flour or grist mills and other manufacturing establishments;
And whereas it is necessary in order to carry out such a scheme of development, that the purchasers should be permitted to construct a storage dam at the outlet of Lake Namekan, at or near Kettle Falls, on the international boundary and to set apart sufficient lands for the construction and maintenance of the said dam, and that they should also, if necessary, he in a position to create storage reservoirs on upper and lower Manitou lake and big Turtle lake under conditions satisfactory to the government by the construction of the necessary dams for that purpose, with the view of maintaining a more regular and uniform flow of water over the falls at Fort Frances, by reinforcing the waters of Rainy lake;
And whereas the construction of the said dams and the maintenance of the waters of Rainy lake at a higher level during the low water period will he of great advantage to navigation;
And whereas it is expedient and desirable, in the interests of the town of Fort Frances, of the said township of Mclrvine and of the public generally, that the said water-power he speedily developed to its full capacity and that an agreement he entered into to that end, upon the terms and subject to the conditions and stipulations herein contained;
And whereas the prrrchasers propose to form a joint stock company under the provisions of the Ontario Companies Act, for the purpose of acquiring this agreement and all the benefits and advantages appertaining thereto, and of assuming the obligations hereby incurred hv the purchaser, and of carrying on the development and operation of the said water-power.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it is abundantly clear that at the request of, and on behalf of Fort Frances this agreement was entered into, and for the very purpose of creating water-power to be used in Canada for the operation of pulp and paper mills. I may now be permitted to state what has happened. I hold in my hand a series of questions that were asked of the company

by the Department of Inland Revenue which has the administration of the expropriation of electricity. Before granting the request of the company for a license, that department, as was quite proper, desired to know from the company how much power they would deliver on the Canadian side, when they would deliver it, and at what price, and on what conditions the Canadian consumer could get it. It was a well known fact that the company had refused to give to any Canadian either mechanical or hydraulic power which could be used for the manufacture of pulp, and the following question was iput to the company.
5. As one of the main natural products ou the Canadian side of the river is pulp-wood, state whether the company or those associated with the company in the manufacture of paper purpose manufacturing pulp-wood into pulp or pulp into paper on the Ontario side of the river as well as on the Minnesota side of the river, and if so, when?
The answer to that was :
The company propose to install a pulp mill on the Canadian side as soon as a pulp-wood concession is granted by the provincial government, which was promised to the company by the late Ross government. The company also propose to erect paper mills on the Canadian side as soon as a pulp concession is secured of sufficient capacity to supply the western Canadian demand.
The impertinence of that answer must be quite apparent to everybody. The Department of Inland Revenue- asked the very plain question, if they intended to erect such works in Ontario, and the answer of the company is : We do if the Ontario government-a government over which this federal government has no control-will give us a pulp concession such as we ask, and we think sufficient to supply the Canadian demand. Now, it was well known at that time that the present government of Ontario had refused to give them or anybody else a pulpwood concession. The policy of the present government in Ontario was. not to give these pulp concessions subject to certain works being erected as had formerly been done but to put them up at public auction, and those who wanted them could ibid on them. The writer of that answer knew perfectly well that there was no possibility of him getting that concession, and I, therefore, say that the answer was extremely impertinent under the circumstances. With regard to concessions, I can speak with knowledge of these early conditions because at that time I represented the community at Fort Frances in the local legislature, and I know the facts. It is true the Ross government did offer this gentleman a concession in 1882 or 1883, but it is also true that he refused to take it. Why? It is very easy to explain why. In the first place, he at that Mr. CONMEE.
time regarded himself, and his associates as the possessors of the only available water-power on the watershed of Rainy Lake, and his words to me were : What advantages would a concession be ; we are obligated to do certain things if we accept, we control the price of wood, nobody else can enter into it, we have the only waterpower in the district. But, Sir, -we all live to learn, and this gentleman learned something later on because it transpired later on that the government of Canada proposed to build a lock at what is known as the Long Sault rapids of the Rainy river in order to improve navigation there. The construction of that lock would involve the building of a dam which would create a considerable water-power, and that might enter into competition with this company. Therefore, we had a revival of the application to get the pulp concession, and other difficulties interposed to prevent the use of the power on the Canadian side. Now,
I will just refer to one more question, question 6 :
If question 5 is answered in the negative, please state whether the use of the grinding room in the Canadian power-house for grinding pulp direct, so as to make the manufacture of pulp by an independent Canadian concern feasible, could be obtained by any Canadian manufacturer desirous of embarking in such an industry, and under what terms and conditions ?
Now, that is a very plain question. Here is the answer:
This would not be practicable, as the company would not allow outsiders to use its power-house. Therefore, in that case the grinders would have to be driven electrically.
That means simply a refusal, because there is no such thing, in a situation such as exists at Fort Frances, of operating pulp-wood grinders by electricity. You have to transform the mechanical power into electric current, then it has to be stepped down, and motors have to be applied, so that the machinery is doubled and the cost is practically doubled. Every manufacturer will understand, without any argument, that that means shutting out any competition whatever with the American company.
Does the hon. gentleman not think that he is discussing the merits of the Bill rather than following the custom on the first reading, of simply explaining the provisions of the Bill?
I will endeavour to comply with the views just expressed. I considered it necessary to make some preliminary remarks as to the conditions that justified the introduction of this as a public Bill.
This is not the time to give those reasons. They may be given on the second reading, but not at this time.

If I had a guarantee that the Bill would reach the second reading, I would be satisfied. Well, to come to the Bill, it proposes to amend chapter 139 of the statutes of 1905, as follow:
Chapter 139 of the Statutes of 1905 is amended by adding after the word 'council* in the last line of section 1 thereof the following: Provided further that the company shall from time to time, if directed by any authority having jurisdiction herein, provide further plans and execute any additional works, alterations or changes, and carry out any new work or works required; or if, upon any application of the town of Fort Frances or otherwise, it shall appear that the company has heretofore constructed, or that the company does at any time hereafter construct or erect any work not approved, the company shall, if directed by any order or ruling, provide plans showing such alterations, changes, additions and new works as may be required by any order or ruling made in pursuance of any such application, and, if so directed by any such order or ruling, execute, perform and carry out all works necessary or required, including the removal of any unauthorized works, if ordered to be removed, and shall, in the execution of such alterations, changes, removals, additions and new works, give full effect to anv such approved plans, and also to the provision of any such order or ruling, not only in regard to the execution of the works or any of them, or other matter incidental thereto, but also in regard to the flow of water for navigation over or through the works of the company, and for the passage of logs and timber, and for the operation of the canal on the Canadian side, the supply of hydraulic power and electrical energy and the regulation of the methods and conditions under which such power and electrical energy shall be furnished to Canadian users, as well as the prices which the company may charge such users for such units ~of power or electrical energy provided for in the said order or ruling.
There are a number of amendments similar to this, none of which change the position of the company under chapter 139, These I submit are matters of public concern and not of a private character. It is not necessarily the duty of a private member to have to undertake an amendment [DOT]of this kind, but I have introduced it at the request of the community of Fort Frances, who feel that their interests are vitally involved, and who feel that they ought to get protection at the hands of parliament-
The hon. gentleman will confine himself to an explanation of the main provisions of the Bill. The merits are discussed on the second reading.
I cannot do that unless I make reference to the laws which it is proposed to amend.
I think it is easy for the hon. gentleman to explain exactly the chief provisions of the Bill.

I have read some of the sections which cover the purport of the Bill as to the regulation- and protection of the public interests in regard to the navigation of the river and as to the works of this company in so far as they affect the public interests. There is another section of the Bill which provides, along the lines of the existing statute, that one-half the total power of the stream created by the works shall be delivered for use on the Canadian side, and that the conditions and prices under which such power may be used shall be regulated either by the Governor in Council or the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada. Either would be acceptable, and that the power shall be supplied either in the form of mechanical power or electrical energy. I submit that parliament never intended to permit these gentlemen to dictate to Canadian users of power in what form they should use it, the Canadian interests are as great in this matter as are the interests of these American gentlemen. The Ontario andi Minnesota company immediately transferred all its rights and interests to an American company incorporated under the laws of the state of Maine, which company is not registered in Canada and has no place of business in Canada. It is that company which is to-day in possession of, and operating these works, and while that company takes all the benefits of the Canadian company, and use the latter as a sort of conduit pipe through which to get favours, it refuses to carry out the obligations imposed by this parliament upon the Canadian company. The object of my amendment is to make it clear that the law may be invoked to compel these gentlemen to carry out their obligation in good faith.
There is another section of the Bill to which I might refer. Every one will admit that I have adduced sufficient evidence to. show that there was to be an equal division of this power. While the town of Fort Francis finds no fault with this company getting its full half of the power of the stream or even more until the power is needed on the Canadian side, what we do say is that we want our position defined and have it definitely decided whether we are entitled to an equal portion of the power. This company says the Canadians are only entitled to one-quarter.
How many horse-power are involved?

About 36,000 horse-power. That is the estimate of this company, but in my humble opinion there can be developed there and utilized 50,000 horsepower. Another clause of this Bill simply provides that the Act of parliament passed by this House in 1905, in which it was said there should be concurrent development and use of the power, be made as was the

284s
evident intention to provide for an equal division of the total power of the stream- and not a division of the Canadian portion of it-and that that principle be carried out and that there shall be a clear declaration that Canadian interests are entitled to one-half of the total power of the stream and entitled to use it under conditions which will admit of its practical use, and that they are not to be denied the right to use mechanical or hydraulic power if it be their interest to do so. They are not to be shut out of the only industry which is natural to their position and for which they have the raw material, namely, the manufacture of pulp and paper.
I submit that these are all matters of a public nature. Although the Bill is said to be a Bill relating to the Ontario and Minneapolis Power Company-I refer now to chapter 139-I submit it is a public Bill. I have read the Bill that company introduced, hon. gentleman can look at it, it will appear in ' Hansard ', and then look at chapter 139 and see that it is a very different Bill. Parliament imposed conditions for the purpose of safeguarding Canadian interests in this water-power, and therefore. whatever may be the title of the Bill, it is in every sense of the word a public Bill, and I submit that this amendment ought to go at least to a committee so that the community at Fort Frances, which has now for ten years been subjected to the very great hardship of sending lawyers and deputations a thousand miles from time to time to protect its interests, may have justice done it by this parliament. If by any technical ruling this measure might be shut out, I hope that there is no member in this House who would take, under these circumstances, a technical objection, and I ask that the measure be allowed its first reading and sent to a committee where it can be threshed out. If any of the provisions of the Bill affect injuriously the private rights of the company, the committee will not tolerate it, and no such measure can pass; but I submit it is a fair measure for removing doubts and difficulties which are due to hasty legislation passed in the manner I have described. One of the clauses of the Act, chapter 139, provides that the Eailway Board of Canada may fix prices and conditions and that application may be made to that board by any applicant for power or by the town of Fort Frances. I submit that every layman would understand by that language that the town of Fort Frances was given the statutory, right to make application to the Eailway Board to have the prices and the conditions fixed in order that the town might be able to say to manufacturers:	Here is the power which you can
have at such prices and under such conditions. But I am told that the town of Fort Francis has been advised that, not-Mr. CONMEE.
withstanding that language, it is doubtful if it could succeed on such an application. The reason given is that under the municipal law it could not apply for power for general purposes. As a town it could apply for power for municipal purposes, but when they go outside of that they might be mpt with difficulty. That is the difficulty raised by the lawyers. I do not know if it be good law or not, but I do know there is sufficient in it to put that small community against this powerful company in a contest in the courts, that it would take six or seven years to determine their rights and they have not the financial ability to do this. Under all the circumstances it seems to me there should be conscience enough in the House of Commons to grant this community some relief from the very perilous condition in which their interests have been placed.

I did not hear the objection to the first reading of the Bill, but it seems to me that the gravamen of it must be that this is a Bill proposing tp amend a private Act. Now, private Bills, including Bills to amend private legislation, require certain notice to be given to the public. Such a Bill must be introduced by petition, but a public Bill may be introduced simply on two days notice in this House. In this case, the public have no notice of what this Bill purports to do, nor have the holders of rights under this private legislation any such notice as is provided for by the rules of this House. It seems to me that this is wrong. I say nothing at present about the desirability of amending the law referred to, or securing the rights of Eainy river; it is simply a question of observing the rules of the House in giving notice of legislation of this kind. There must be, I take it, vested rights grown up under the Act of incorporation, and this proposed Bill would affect such rights.
If I may be permitted to answer the hon. member: I do not think he was in his place at the opening of my remarks.
I was not.

I showed that, under sec. 18 of the Eevised Statutes of Canada, of 1906, all Bills are public Bills,-that section states so in so many words; I do not need to read it again. And I showed by quotations from Bourinot what the practice of this House has been. A number of public Bills amending private Acts have been passed in this House. I do not know that I have prepared myself fully for an argument on the rules of parliament in that respect, but, so far as I have been able to examine-and I have consulted some of the gentlemen who are in charge of the

committees, and who have had a good deal of experience-the opinion seems to be that the procedure is quite regular. And, so far as notice is concerned, I can tell my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule), that notice of this question has been before the public for years. The newspapers of Fort Frances are full of it; the company has had written notice,-I saw to it myself that they should know exactly what was done. And there is lots of time for anything of that kind. This Bill will have to go to committee, and it will be some time before it reaches the House again. No one will be taken by surprise, and no interest can possibly be prejudiced for want of all the notice necessary.
Mr. LANCASTER, I do not think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oonmee), has quite appreciated the objection made by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule). If he has, I think that I personally should interpose here. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Conmee), if there is any merit in his Bill, is seeking to amend a private Act. The hon. gentleman cannot evade the rules of the House, and introduce what is, in fact, a private Bill, of which notice should be given, by merely declaring it a public Bill. If this were introduced as a private Bill, notice in the form which is well known, would have to be given to the public so that those interested -would have a chance to be heard. These rules are made for a purpose, and are always carried out, for our -procedure in relation to private Bills is different from that in relation to public Bills.	[DOT]
And there are fees to be paid.

Yes, there are fees to be paid and all sorts of things to be done in the case of a private Bill. It seems to me that the hon. member for Thunder Bay and Rainy River (Mr. Conmee), is trifling with the intelligence of this House in taking up time with this matter. I thinlf the whole thing is out of order, because it must be apparent to you, Mr. Speaker, as to every member of the House, that the hon. gentleman is introducing what is really private legislation, and ought to be introduced in accordance with the rules applying to legislation of that kind. He had no right to introduce it as he did and call it a public Bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I pointed out to my hon. friend (Mr. Conmee), that the purpose disclosed by the notice which he gave, and which appears on the order paper is to introduce ' an Act to amend chapter 139, 4 and 5, Edward VII., intituled an Act respecting the Ontario and Minnesota Power Company, Limited.' The Act to be amended is undoubtedly a private Act. It is quite true that all Acts passed
by this parliament are public Acts; but it is equally true also that there are two categories of public Acts,, one known as private Acts, to be introduced in this House in accordance with certain rules, and not to be amended except in the same manner. My hon. friend (Mr. Conmee), has quoted some authorities which go to show that private Acts may foe amended by public Bills in some matters which are not essential, which are not part of the parliamentary contract,-for a private Act is a parliamentary contract and is to be amended only under the rules which have been provided by parliament for the security of private parties. My own impression, at first blush, is that the Bill proposed by my hon. friend certainly interferes with the corporate powers of a private company and is, therefore, to foe introduced only in accordance with the rules relating to private legislation. But, if I may be permitted, I would suggest that the Bill be read the first time, and the question whether it is a private Bill or not, should be settled by you, Mr. Speaker, before the-next- reading.
MrTLANCASTER. If I am in order: I would point out that it would, I fear, be trifling with the rules of the House to let the Bill go in that way. I think that the first reading should stand for the consideration which the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), proposes. We should be stultifying ourselves to let the first reading go through when the rules declare that it should not go through. I think the point ought to be decided.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is for Mr. Speaker.

I am prepared to say now that my impression is, after hearing the explanation of the hon. gentleman and reading the provisions concerning - the company, that this is purely a private Bill, and so comes Under Rules 88, 89 and so on and must be introduced by petition, the fees paid and the other formalities that are provided for, observed. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Conmee), wishes a more elaborate opinion, I will be able to give it tomorrow, setting forth the definition of private Bills, the precedents and so on. In the meantime, I may briefly quote Bouri-not:
Private Bills are distinguished from public Bills in that they directly relate to the affairs of private individuals or of corporate bodies, and not to matters of public policy or to the community in general. They must pass through the same stages as public Bills, but, at the same time, must originate by petition and be subject to certain, special standing orders in both Houses of parliament.
There can be no doubt that this Bill merely relates to the community residing-

in Fort Frances and its immediate vicinity, and not to the community generally. In another place, Bourinot describes this class of Bill:
Bills from the corporation of towns and municipal bodies, generally, are always treated as private Bills when they desire special legislation affecting their proper interests.
This is such a case, I submit, and therefore I cannot allow the Bill to be introduced. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Conmee), will have to comply with the rule of the House. I will give a more elaborate opinion to-morrow if necessary.
Motion ruled out of order,

speakeroldname: Mr. J. D. TAYLOR (New Westminster) moved:
speechtext:
For a return showing all applications for homestead or pre-emption in the railway belt in the district of New Westminster, with names of applicants, and description of proposed location^ pending at the time of the recent suspension of the regulations governing the disposal of these lands; also any order or orders in council by virtue of which these regulations have stood suspended during 1910.
He said: While this motion as offered refers only to the riding of New Westminster, the conditions there indicated are common throughout the whole railway belt in British Columbia and have constituted during the past year a very serious grievance to persons who have approached British Columbia with a view to taking up residence there. I may say that in no other year since confederation have there been so many persons looking towards British Columbia as a place of future Mr. PATERSON.
residence, and yet we find that in this year, the year of all others when the Department of the Interior and its officers should have been alert in guiding applicants for location in British Columbia towards the land there, the railway belt has been completely locked up without, any warrant whatever in law, as I say, after diligent inquiry made of the Department of the Interior. We find the origin of the trouble to be in a new set of regulations sprung upon the public early in the spring without any notification whatever even to the agents of the department in British Columbia that anything of the kind was in contemplation. The result of these new regulations if they had gone into effect would have been to kill every one of the hundreds of applications sent into the department for locations in that province. However, at the time set for these regulations to go into effect an order in council was passed suspending their operation until a time to be stated in the future, a time which has not yet been stated, so that during the whole of the active season of 1910 we have been in British Columbia without any regulations whatever applicable to the land in the railway belt. I say without any regulations applicable but the fact that the administration is paralyzed appears to be due to the personal act of the Minister of the Interior, because when the new regulations were suspended it is quite plain to any one who studies the situation that the old regulations in the absence of any interference with them by law by any other agency than the proposed new' regulations must continue in effect. Still while by law they are in; effect we find that by the personal order of the Minister of the Interior, I presume, because it is in his department, by some order not communicated by order in council or in any other public manner, the land agents throughout British Columbia were instructed not to receive any applications whatever, not to deal with a bit of land in any way, not to give any

satisfaction to any one of the hundreds of persons who have applications pending before those agents for homesteads, on many of which they have been living but who find themselves now without any warrant that they will at any time secure the patents to these lands. The subject is not one which calls for any lengthy remarks, but I do submit that it calls for the attention of the House in view of the extraordinary condition revealed that by the arbitrary act of one minister the settlement of a whole province can be retarded for a season, and a most active season at that.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Before the motion passes, I would like to draw the attention of the mover (Mr. Taylor, New Westminster) to a difficulty in meeting the request contained in the motion. The motion asks for a return showing all applications for homestead or pre-emption in the railway belt in the district of New Westminster, with names of applicants and description of proposed locations, &c. There may be record in the departments of applications which have been made, but my hon. friend will be aware that there is a great possibility of very many applications having been made of -which we have no record, and, therefore, we are not able to give him the information. In the ordinary course of the transaction of business at the land offices an application would be made verbally and there would toe no record of its having been made ; so that, while we are willing and anxious to give the hon. member all information in this connection, I desire to point out the difficulty that there is in giving him a large amount of information on the point that he particularly asks about.
In regard to his remarks on the subject in general, I would like to point out that he has rather misunderstood the question when he says that there has been no dealing with homestead entries in the railway belt for the past year. There has been no suspension of the regulations, and no suspension of activity in dealing with homestead lands in that part of the railway belt known as the dry section, that is to say, in the section of which Kamloops is the centre. In that area there has been a continuous movement in the way of dealing in homestead rights and my hon. friend, I think has been certainly quite misinformed when he gave us to understand that there had been no issuing of homestead rights during the year. "	[DOT]
May I ask the minister whether these dealings were under the old regulations or under the new regulations?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Under the old regulations. To explain to the House fully, if I may take
the time, the reason for the condition of which my hon. friend complains in other sections of the railway toelt, the difficulties that have to be met in the administration are these : In the district of New Westminster, as well as in the district eastward of the dry belt, owing to the activity of investors in lumber, not absolutely all, but practically all the land that is suitable for homesteading in those sections of the railway toelt has been covered by licenses to cut timber. The general condition in those sections of the railway belt is that in order to give a homestead entry the land has to be withdrawn from the timber berth. There are exceptions to the rule, but my hon. friend is well aware that the exceptions are only exceptions, and do not cover any important section of the conditions existing. As the House is aware, the timber in the railway belt is of very great value, partly because of the great size of the trees, and partly because of the nearness to transportation facilities by reason of the existence of the railway, and for other reasons. When we have to deal with the question of settlers' rights in that way we have to deal with it very cautiously and carefully. While we are anxious that the lumberman shall not hold his license for lands that are proper to be settled upon, at the same time we desire to be careful not to withdraw from him, or to aid anybody else in any action that would result in causing to be withdrawn from him, those rights to the timber for which he has paid, and thereby cause the undue destruction of timber which is a most valuable asset of this country. The difficulties of the situation are such that they have been engaging the attention of the Department of the Interior for several years and, as the result of this consideration, some time in the early part of last summer, certain regulations were issued for the information of the public looking to the adjustment of these difficulties between settlegs and limit holders that, it was hoped, would be at any rate, moderately satisfactory, and would "tend to the further development of the country without undue *trespass upon the rights of any one. These regulations were issued early in the summer time, and were to go into effect, I think, on the 1st July, so that there should toe ample notice to everybody before they would come into effect as to what their character was. Not at all unexpectedly, objections were offered to these regulations, and in view of the objections that were made and of the very complicated and difficult character of the question that had to be dealt with it was thought advisable to give the matter further consideration, and to suspend the regulations until that still further consideration had been given and until all interests concerned had been further consulted. That is the matter as it

stands up to the present time. It is not correct to say that the suspension of these regulations has 'been any serious deterrent to settlement in the railway belt because there cannot in the nature of things be any serious accession to settlement in the railway belt until the question of timber rights, the respective rights of the lumber holders, and of the (prospective homesteaders, have been properly adjusted. As long as the limits stay as they are there cannot be any serious amount of homesteading in the sections of the railway belt which have been held under reservation. It may be said that entries might have been given in the small portions of those sections which are not covered by timber berths. It seemed to the government that it was advisable-for it seemed to be necessary to make a radical change in the method of the disposition of rights to settlers-that there should be no distinction drawn between the small area outside of the timber berths, and the large area inside the timber berths ; that is to say if it was sound public policy to enter upon a new system in dealing with homesteads in the railway belt it was right and proper that all should be put upon the same basis. So the matter has had to await further consideration with reference to all the interests affected. My hon. friend is aware, I presume, that we expect to have the opportunity of consulting a very representative delegation of one of those interests in a short time, and we hope after that consultation to be able to take such action as will relieve the present situation of which my hon. friend complains.

If the new regulations were to be proclaimed tomorrow what would be the fate of the persons whose applications for homesteads are now pending? Would they be dealt with under the old regulations or under the new regulations?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is a matter that is the subject of consideration at the present time. If the regulations which were promulgated in the early part of last summer to take effect on the 1st July as they stand were to go into effect to-morrow ali applications not already dealt with would be dealt with under those new regulations.

Mr. Speaker, if nobody else wishes to discuss the motion I would like to point out to the minister one or two defects in his answer. In the first place, what he has said just now in reply to my question touches the crux of the whole situation, that there are in the district of New Westminster alone a great many applications for homesteads pending, and they have been pending for not a few months, but for many years, through no fault of the applicants, but simply because of Mr. OLIVER.
the dilatoriness which characterizes the conduct of business in the Department of the Interior so far as the Canadian Pacific railway is concerned. Some of these applicants for homesteads have been pushing their claims for from 10 to 15 years to my knowledge. The minister's flies are stacked with correspondence from me (luring the last few months, calling -his attention to case after case of this nature, where men have been trying for years to get their papers, where they know of no obstacle except the dilatoriness of the department, and where they are left in this state of uncertainty now; that if the regulations are proclaimed their last chance of securing these homesteads disappears, according to the statement just made by the minister, a statement which confirms the worse fears of these homesteaders and their apprehensions which have been the basis of the many protests delivered to the minister during the last few months. I would like to point out to the minister also that he misjudges the quantity of land available for settlement in the railway belt in the district of New Westminster. In one breath he tells us that the applications are so numerous that he cannot bring down a complete return because there are so many made by word of mouth as well as in writing. I think he will admit that when a man goes into the land office in New Westminster and makes an application for land, that he applies for a definite piece of land. I know of any number of cases where men have gone in with a definite application for a piece of land only to be told that there is nothing doing at all, that the agent will not receive the application for that or for any other land, and that the agent will not give any idea as to when the applicant may come back. I know also that the minister, only last year, gave away by private treaty to a quartette of favourites in Vancouver no less than 6,800 acres in one block in the district of New Westminster; gave away these 6,800 acres available for settlement upon which applicants for homesteads would gladly have gone; gave them away at the ridiculous price of $1.50 per acre, land which could be sold at an instant's notice to-day for $150 an acre or more; and gave those lands away .on the sole promise that there was some great dyking scheme in connection with it. I do not know what information the minister had upon which to base that transaction. I made some inquiries last year and was told that the department had no information at all as to the value of land in that vicinity. A short time before that a small parcel of land in the same neighbourhood was handed out to a political favourite at a price much below the market value and inquiry was made in this House as to whether or not there were" any more

lands available in that district at less than the schedule price named by the department. The answer was that there was no other land available at any reduced price, which was a warning' to all persons concerned to make no application for snaps of that kind. And yet, hard on the heels of that statement that no other land was available at anything less than the regular price, we fipd this transaction (at a still lower price) with an organization in Vancouver closely identified with the famous Bob Kelly whose name as the head of the British Columbia Tammany is now being heralded in the press of the continent. Now, I ask why the minister tells us today that there is no considerable quantity of land available in the railway belt for settlement for the small man who wants 160 acres, or, the 20 acres or 40 acres to be allowed under the new regulations, when onl" a year ago he was handing it out in 6,800 acre blocks to the associates of Bob Kelly.
At how much per acre?

I have already told the House at $1.50 per acre, subiect to conditions of dyking, conditions similar to those observed without any order in council or any Act of parliament by every farmer on the delta land in British Columbia; conditions which will bring to this aggregation of favourites from Vancouver a profit which may be moderately estimated at $1,000,000. One million dollars, Mr. Speaker, to be handed out without notice, without competition to a few favourites from Vancouver, speculators in land; while the department does not know of any more lands available there as to which it is worth while to give their attention to satisfy the demands of men who wish to become bona fide settlers.
What is the date of the grant?

The date of the information about no other land being available would be about 1907, the date of the grant was in 1909, barely two years afterwards, and the lands in question are almost adjoining although the answer given to this House was that there was no other land in the vicinity to be obtained at anything less than the price laid down by the department. Now, Mr. Speaker, I submit that the minister should revise his answers and should find some other reason for tieing up' settlement in the district of New Westminster; I submit that he should take the House into his confidence and tell who are these fortunate people in the dry belt in British Columbia who had influence enough to cause the suspension of these regulations that were proclaimed
early in 1910. He might give us some shadow of reason why conspicious friends of the government in the dry belt should be able to have regulations suspended while their special cases are being dealt with, while at the same time people in the lower mainland of British Columbia, who have no other claim than that they are honest citizens and intending homesteaders, are turned away from his land offices with the statement that this government will not give any attention to their requests.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend asks how it is that, having said to the House that we had no land to sell in the lower railway belt, we afterwards sold some.

Not quite' that. The question asked in the House was whether there was any other land in the vicinity of this land on Pitt Meadows, for sale at less than the prices laid down by law or by regulation of the department. The answer was, no, but hard upon the heels of that answer came a sale of 6,800 acres to the quartette of political favourites.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The question of my hon. friend sounds like an echo of the cele^ brated Robins Irrigation debate that occurred in this House. My hon. friend asks in regard to the sale of certain marsh lands at a price. We are not selling marsh lands at a price any more than we are selling irrigation lands at a price. It is true that an amount is paid, but that is not the price that we sell the land at. The price is the money that is paid plus the cost of the reclamation of the land. We sold some at the price my hon. friend mentions plus the cost of reclamation. We were asked if vve had any more to sell. We had not any more to sell; we have no land to sell for money in the lower railway belt. But we had land to sell for reclamation, and we sold it for reclamation. It is being reclaimed, I believe, and my hon. friend will not deny that the reclamation of that land means a very great increase in the value of thi; land in his constituency, and is for the benefit of the country as well. If my hon. friend is horrified at the idea of our selling marsh lands at $1.50 an acre plus the cost of reclamation, I will tell him that there is still other marsh land in his constituency, of which he knows very well, a very large area of it, which four years a'go we offered for sale-if he likes to put it that way, although I do not put it that way-not at $1.50 an acre, but several thousand acres for one dollar plus the cost of reclamation.
Not to political favourites That was towards a public undertaking.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Precisely. It was an offer to constituents of my hon. friend or of his colleague for purposes of reclamation; and if he finds fault with us for having sold this other land at $1.50 an acre, in what position must we stand in his estimation [DOT] for having offered several thousand acres at the price of a single dollar plus the cost of reclamation? And the land, has not yet been sold nor the reclamation made.
The conditions were entirely different.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I will admit that the conditions were somewhat different, but not entirely different. In the one case the land was marsh, in the other case it was partly _ marsh and partly lake. In both cases it was not land capable of cultivation without reclamation; in both cases large expenditures to secure reclamation were necessary. Because a less cost would be incurred in reclaiming the land in the one case than in the other, we charged $1.50 an acre, in the one case and only one dollar for several thousand acres in the other case. The reclamation in the one case is going forward, and I believe will be successful, while in the other case, although the land was offered practically for nothing, it appears not to be worth the cost of reclamation.
_ Mr. TAYLOR (New Westminster). My information about a month ago on the spot was that the reclamation was going forward.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The bargain was made four years ago, and the last I heard of it was that the reclamation was not going forward. If the hon. gentleman has knowledge that it is, no one will be more pleased than I.
The minister refers to Sumas lake?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
The minister must know that he renewed that last year.	.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Under such an arrangement as I speak of the land was for a time in the hands of the strongest financial company in British Columbia, unless the Canadian Pacific railway itself, and yet it has not been reclaimed unless it has been done recently.	G	.
The minister knows why that company gave it up?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I only know they gave it up. But if the company fulfil the conditions required and reclaim that land, I am prepared to defend the transaction in this House or anywhere else, and I am sat-Mr. TAYLOR (New Westminster).
isfied the House would uphold the action l took.
Motion agreed to.
Before the orders of the day are called, I would ask what progress has been made in the printing of the proceedings of the farmers delegation which met here on the 16th of December last.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I will take a note of my hon. friends request and ask the Secretary of State.

subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.

speechtext: Mr. VERVILLE moved third reading of Bill (No. 3), respecting the hours of labour on public works.

subtopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
I had not the privilege of being present when the amended Bill was discussed a couple of weeks ago, not having returned from the Pacific coast after our adjournment; but on reading the report of the debate on that occasion, I saw some remarks which I think ought not to pass unchallenged. I read for instance, the statement by the hon. gentleman in whose name this Bill stands (Mr. Verville)., that he had received from several labour organizations, particularly in Montreal,. petitions or memorials or other documentary evidence in favour of the Bill in its present form. At the outset I wish to say, in order to remove any apprehension, that I am not opposing this Bill; because the very smallest movement in the direction of recognizing an eight hour day, is better than no progress at all; but I noticed that the hon. gentleman did not specify what labour organizations had petitioned in favour of his amended Bill and what workmen there were who preferred this amended measure to the sturdy effort made by him in the first place. A great many members in this House have received petitions in connection with this Bill, but, so far as I am aware, these petitions relate solely to the Bill introduced last fall and not to its substitute. I do think that it would have been only just to this House for any representative of labour, who had a mandate from any labour organization to accept this substituted Bill, to have given us the address of the people for whom he spoke. I do not think that it is right that an hon. member should come here speaking as a representative of labour and leave us in any doubt as to the position of the great labour organizations in this country with respect to legislation of this kind; and you must realize that the bare statement by any hon. gentleman that he had received petitions from labour organizations does not carry nearly so much

weight as if he stood up here with the documents in his hand and read them to the House., spread them on the pages of * Hansard ', and allowed us to jee hy whom they were signed and what class of labouring imen were content with so small a measure of justice. I have a number of petitions with respect to this Bill \yhich 1 shall not present to the House in an anonymous way, but will either read or give the addresses of the organizations which have sent them. In the case of a very few, I shall read the petitions themselves because they are rather important in their nature. I have first one, from the Trades and Labour Council at Vancouver, dated the 2nd of January, which reads as follows :
J. D. Taylor, M.P.,
House of Commons, Ottawa.
Dear Sir :-I am instructed by the Vancouver Trades and Labour Council to again draw your attention to the fact that this central labour union has repeatedly placed itself upon record as being unequivocally in favor of the enactment of a federal eight-hour day, along the lines of the Bill introduced by Alphonse Ver-ville, M.P. Having this in mind, we will not burden you with further resolutions upon the subject, but desire to impress upon your mind that wage workers of western Canada are deeply concerned in the passage of such a measure. We heartily endorse the expressions and position taken by the members of the executive committee of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada wbo appeared before this special committee dealing with the subject some months ago. We further believe that the tendency of this day and age is towards a shorter work day; this, because the workers rightly feeL. that they should participate in some of the benefits accruing from the introduction of modern machinery. In fact, there are so few arguments against the enactment of such a measure that it seems needless for us to go any further into the question at this time. Trusting that we may have the pleasure of a hearing from you at the earliest possible date, -with regard to your attitude on this question.
(Signed) R. P. PETTIPIECE, Secretary.

Dear Sir,-Through a unanimous vote of my local, I have been instructed to ask for your moral support on the eight-hour Bill presented by Mr. A. Verville, M.P. Hoping you will condescend to back this most needed legislation.

Secretary.
Here is another from the Montreal Union of Carpenters and Joiners of America, No. 178; and still another from the Montreal International Association of Machinists, as follows:
Labour Temple, 303 St. Dominique St. Hon. Member.
Dear Sir,-The Bill No. 3 entitled ' An Act concerning the hours of labour on public works/ presented by Mr. Alphonse Verville, will soon come before the House for discussion.
We wish to inform you that our union, after carefully studying this Bill, has decided to support it and respectfully ask you to approve of it by giving it your vote.
You probably know that for a number of years the labour movement, not only in the province of Quebec but in the whole Dominion, has demanded this humanitarian and indispensable measure under the existing situation.	.
The investigation made by your special committee on this important question has proved without a doubt -that the objections raised affected principally the contracts for transportation by land or water, on the other hand the evidence given in favour of the Bill were well founded.
Hoping you will accede to our request and we may count you amongst the supporters of the Bill No. 3.
We remain yours,

I have here another from the Journeymen Tailors' Union of America, Local 137 Montreal. The Montreal Trades and Labour Council-speaking, I presume, for the body of labour .generally in the ' citv of Montreal-sends the following;

Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-At the last meeting of the Trades and Labour Council held on Thursday, Decern-ber 15, 1910, a resolution was adopted asking your support on behalf of the 8-hour Bill presented by Mr. Alphonse Verville, M.P.

The communication from the Journeyman Stonecutters' Association of North America. Montreal branch, is as follows:

Montreal, Dec. 24, 1910.
Dear Sir,-At a meeting of the Montreal Branch of the Journeymen Stone Cutters' Association of North America, held at. Montreal, December 21, the 8-hours Bill introduced in the House of Commons by Alphonse Verville, M.P., was read.
