The Montreal Branch of the J. S. C. A. of N.A.
GEO. DURANT A YE, Secretary.
There is another from the International Union of Working Barbers, Montreal Local. The National Trades and Labour Council of Quebec writes as follows:
Quebec, January 21, 1911.

Would the hon. member telL the House what- has been the effect in practice of having those words in that legislation, and to what extent the courts have found it possible to enforce the Act owing to those words?

I am sorry if the minister, having such valuable information in his possession, has neglected the many opportunities he has had of presenting it to me and to this House, so as to enlighten our ignorance on this most important subject.

The hon. member is trying to evade my question. The information is there, and if he has read the report he will see that the effect of those words has been practically to nullify the legislation. The courts found it so, and I call upon him to deny it, if it is not true.

I am making an address now on Mr. Skelton's evidence before a special committee of this House; I am not denying or affirming any proposition put forward by the Minister of Labour, but I do say he has been distinctly derelict in his duty if, having information of this kind in his possession, he has been so careless, so indifferent and so absolutely sure that he can get a majority of this House to do whatever any ministers of the Crown tell them they are to do, that it is not necessary for him to give any reasonable excuse for any course he suggests to them. Section 2 reads:-

That any officer or agent of the government of the United States or of the District of Columbia, or any contractor, or sub-contractor, whose duty it shall be to employ, direct, or control any labourer or mechanic employed upon any of the public works of the United States or of the District of Columbia who shall intentionally violate any provision of this Act shall be deemed guilty of a misdemeanour and for each and every offence, upon conviction, be punished by a fine not to exceed one thousand dollars or by imprisonment for not more than six months, or by both, such fine and imprisonment in the discretion of the court having Jurisdiction thereof.
The third section provides that the Act does not apply to pending contracts. _ Mr. Macdonell, a member of the committee, then asks:-
Is there any other exception than the emei gency exception.
Professor Skelton-No exception.
The United States, having had experience for some time 'with this Act, and not having recognized the calamity that the use of the words ' or permit ' had brought upon them, according to the Minister of Labour to-day, proceeded to pass supplementary legislation nine years afterwards. But these Americans are slow; it takes them a long time to recognize that this is a misfortune to them. Prof. Skelton, at page 24, reports:
Letter carriers may be required to work as nearly as practicable only eight hours on each working day, but not in any event exceeding forty-eight hours during the six working days of each week; and such number of hours, on Sunday, not exceeding eight, as may be required by the needs of the service- and if a legal holiday shall occur on auy working day the service performed on such day, if less than eight hours, shall be counted as eight hours without regard to the time actually employed.	.
This Act was passed m 1901. The following year, that is in the session of 1901-2, the eight-hour law was explicitly declared to apply to all irrigation works undertaken by the secretary of the Interior.
So well satisfied was the congress of the United States with the operation of this Act after it had been in force nine years that instead of weakening it, instead of withdrawing it, instead of whittling it down until it meant nothing whatever it deliberately proceeded to extend it. The report proceeds :
In 1905-1906 when the Panama canal was being planned it was enacted that the provisions of the Act of 1892, the long one which I read, should not apply to unskilled alien labcurers and to the foremen and superintendents of such labourers employed in the construction of the Isthmian canal. . . To summarize, the federal government has provided that eight hours shall constitute the limit that may be required or permitted of any workman, mechanic or labourer in its own immediate employment whether engaged in erecting public buildings or fortifications-public works Mr. TAYLOR (New Westminster).
in the ordinary sense-constructing the vast irrigation works which are now being undertaken in the semi-arid west, or if they are citizens or skilled aliens, employed on the Panama canal; they are all in direct government employ. If they are employed in the government navy yards, arsenals or ordnance factories, or in the public printing bureau or engaged as letter carriers-I should omit letter carriers, that is a special .provision-they ail have the obligatory eight-hour day.
The proceedings of this special committee were carried on during very many weeks and such a mass of evidence was presented by persons for or against the Bill that it was suggested that the committee should call upon Professor Skelton again to help them to come to a conclusion. Mr. Skelton was examined as to the result of the studies which he had carried on independently during the period of the committee's activities. He was examined by a former labour member in this House in the person of Mr. Smith. He was asked about a specific law in Australia, and he said that :
The nearest approach in New Zealand to the legislation contemplated by the Bui before us is the Public Contracts Act of 1900, which provides that in all contracts above 20 pounds in value, for the construction or repair of public works or for any public service in which manual labour is needed, .current fair wages shall be paid and an eight-hour day observed. The discussion in the House when this Act was passed showed that it was designed to force on all contractors, particularly in outlying districts, where roads, bridges and culverts were being built, the hours customary in better organized districts. The eight-hour specified was, in view of the prevalence of the eight-hour standard, practically a fair hours provision. Overtime, more-ovpt is allowed.
That is on 'page 367. Then, on page 373, Professor Skelton hazards this suggestion :
If it is felt desirable that the Dominion shculd use the means at its disposal

I would call the attention of the Minister of Labour to this. This is his own witness.

I think the hon. member is utterly mistaken when he speaks of Professor Skelton as my own witness. Professor Skelton was brought before the committee at the request of the committee itself. The committee was composed of gentlemen opposite as well as gentlemen on this side of the House. He was not in any way the witness of any one particular member of the committee.

That opens another subject upon which I willingly would not have entered. That opens the subject of the procuring of Professor Skelton, and what I claim to Ibe double * dealing in this House in connection with

the procuring. 1 have the evidence in this book in my hand, and if I wanted to take up the time of the House I could read it, that Professor Skelton was retained three weeks before the Minister of Labour came into this House to ask permission to retain an expert from outside to assist the committee. I have 'the statement in this book that he was retained in consequence, and as a result of a conference between the Minister of Labour and the right hon. First Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and that the clerk of the House was consulted, presumably by the Minister of Labour, as to whether or not the committee had authority to engage this professor without referring to the House. I have the professor's own statement that he was communicated with by telephone. I would ask whether the members of the committee had a specially arranged telephone with one horn to the ear of each member of the committee, one speaking piece for each member, or whether they jointly spoke to this professor two days before he was engaged, or whether it was some responsible minister, some person with some show of authority, who engaged the professor, who talked with him over the 'phone two days before he was actually engaged, and told him to get busy and prepare for a formal call from this committee. I say it is trifling with the intelligence of this House, it is presuming too much upon the carelessness of the members of this House, this action having been taken in the hope of members not having read the contents of this book for the minister to attempt to lead us to believe that he was not personally concerned in the retaining of Professor Skelton.

I am sure the hon. member does not intend to be other than'fair or that he would not like to have the House feel that he did not intend to be fair. Every statement which he has made may be quite correct, but the implication which he has tried to make, is not an accurate one. I can state the facts to the hon. member, and if I am in error hon. gentlemen who were members of this committee can correct me. Some of them are present and are sitting opposite. It was suggested in the committee before the Christmas recess, that some one should be engaged to compile the legislation of different countries, and advise us as to how this legislation had worked out in practice. An officer of the Department of Labour was not called in, not because there were not men in the department, officers who could do the work, but because it was thought that it might be considered that evidence given by an officer of the department was ex parte evidence in favour of one class. That the subject was one affecting all classes and that exception might be taken by manufacturers or farmers to evidence from such a source. The committee thought, and rightly, I think, that there should be an impartial third person engaged, and a university professor who was interested neither one way nor the other, and who was well qualified for the work, was selected. The situation when the "House adjourned for the Xmas recess was that we had either to delay until the House resumed after the recess, or retain his services forthwith so that he might have an opportunity during the recess of parliament, which was also his recess, of dealing with the matter. It was impossible for me as a member oi the committee to, on my own responsibility, appoint this gentleman or on behalf of the committee without making sure that his appointment would be confirmed later on. When the committee suggested, so that there might be no delay in a full and complete investigation, that I should try and arrange to have Professor Skelton do that work during the Christmas vacation, I consulted the Prime Minister and the clerk of the House to ascertain whether such would be a proper course, and whether if I acceded to the wishes oi the committee I might feel sure that the. House would support me. Having consulted the Prime Minister, that right hon. gentleman said, that if anything could be done to expedite the Tyork, and carry out the wishes of the committee it should be done. With that authority I told Professor Skelton that I had assurances which I considered satisfactory to guarantee he would be retained, and that it would meet the wishes of the committee if he would agree to undertake the work forthwith. If the hon. gentleman can find anything not in accordance with the facts in that statement I challenge him to |do so. But, the hon. gentleman is acting unfairly when he makes insinuation after insinuation, with the view of misleading every member in this House
Order.
The Minister of Labour had better withdraw that statement.
The last statement made by the minister should be modified.
If I used language I should not have used I certainly withdraw it immediately.

To avoid misunderstanding I wish to repeat inferentially everything I have said in this House, and. to challenge the Minister oi Labour to point to one sentence which I cannot make absolutely good from the records. I have listened patiently to the oration from the Minister of Labour, and I am not surprised that he shows heat; if I were in his position I think I would


show even more heat. But I would like to * ask him why he took up so much time to combat the statement I hazarded, that 'Professor Skelton was his witness, while the result of his effort was only to corroborate that statement in every detail. There is no doubt whatever in my mind that the Minister of Labour was the member of that 'committee who named Professor Skelton.
I	think I am entitled to assume that Professor Skelton was his witness, and the Minister of Labour has no right to refer ~to that as an insinuation. I say it is a fair assumption from all the circumstances.
II	have no direct knowledge as to whether Professor Skelton was his witness or the -witness of the Prime Minister, but I think a fair assumption from this report is that lie was the choice of the Minister of La->l>our, and the Minister of Labour having
[DOT]i" i bin, to offer his advice has a right to take that advice. However, this is what Professor Skelton says:
Tf it is felt desirable that the Dominion should use the means at its disposal, however limited, to set the pace, the path of least resistance it is generally recognized lies along the adoption of the eight-hour day in government employment

Not mark you only on public buildings under contract, but in government employment.
-and the insertion of an eight-hour clause for contracts on public works. Possibly the adoption of a fair hour's supplement to the fair wages clause might be discussed in thai connection.
To that extent, the professor bears out The contention put forward from this side [DOT] of the House, that if the government really [DOT]desired to secure an eight-hour day for ; government employment they could have [DOT]d-one it themselves without any of this :meaningless parade. Now, then, this witness called by the Minister of Labour proceeds :
If the committee decide to make the application of this Bill-
He was stopped short there. This processor having studied the question, having thoroughly mastered 400 pages of in-'.forination, being under the impression that he was called in to enable the committee to do something, proceeded to give his ad-wice whatever it might be worth, as to what they might most advantageously do, -when he was stopped by the Minister of I.abour, the very man who asked this House to submit the Bill to the committee so that the committee might perfect the Bill, and remove the disadvantages which would have arisen. I challenged the Minister of Labour to say whether he would [DOT]cause that committee to report back the Bill or whether he would not, and he answered me at that time in the most arro-Mr. TAYLOR (New Westminster).
gant way that it was an improper assumption on my part that he or any other member of the committee had any other idea than to report back the Bill to the House; and yet, this very man, being offered by his own witness a suggestion as to the kind of Bill he should report, stops him with this remark:
The Chairman. The committee has'nt any decision to make on that point.
Prof. Skelton. You meau as to the interpretation of the term 'public works'?
The professor could not believe his ears; he could not believe he was in the presence of the assassin of the Bill. The Minister of Labour said:
The committee, of course, is simply concerned with this Bill of Mr. Verville's; we have nothing to do with the framing of the law itself, but if you are dealing with anything other than what is included in that Bill

The meaning of the Minister of Labour was: For goodness sake, Mr. Professor, we are getting along very nicely now, we have got this thing so beclouded that nobody but yourself can make such a summary of all this evidence as you are making; if you present this summary to us, and tell us all what it means it will be incumbent upon us to report this Bill this session, so for goodness sake don't do it, and he did not do it. Mr. Speaker, he was not permitted to do it. Then Professor Skelton sa id:
"Well, would it be

He only got this far when he was stopped again by the Minister of Labour so anxious was 'he that this professor should not give that committee too much enlightenment. Of course the shorthand reporter did not get down the whole dramatic scene; you would need a moving picture machine to do that in detail, but something happened between the pauses, and so the Minister of Labour1 said:
The Chairman.-I beg your pardon, I interrupted you, perhaps I may have misunderstood what you were going to say.
A. I was going to make some suggestions in the event of the Bill applying to public works, hut perhaps that is not needed at this stage.
The Chairman.-That is quite proper; if your observations have led you to believe there are certain features which should be considered in connection with our public works, you certainly should give them.
This professor had been invited to make a recommendation. Not spontaneously invited. This thing did not occur all of itself. The committee were very coy about receiving advice from the professor; but finally they prevailed upon themselves to receive some information from him, and this is what they got:

A. Well, quite aside from the question, whether it is feasible to adopt an eight-hour day even on public works, I would like to say, if it were adopted there are some considerations which a study particularly of the American conditions have suggested. So that without prejudice to the question of the advisability of any such law at all I think it is clear that it would be better in framing such a measure to make a positive enumeration of the trades to which it should apply rather than to make a sweeping statement and then to insert exception after exception as to the trades to which it should apply. Again, if it were applied to public buildings I think some such provision should be inserted as that embodied in the Wisconsin law which provides that the provisions of the Act should be confined to work done on the spot, not to the preparation of materials necessary. It would have to be considered, too, whether an eight-hour day meant a 48-hour week or a 44-hour week, that is, the question of the short hours on Saturday might come in. The question of overtime is also a difficult matter. It might be possible to penalize overtime by requiring higher pay for extra hours, but the danger of this, of course, is that "with such a provision in the Bill, it becomes not an Act to enforce shorter hours, but an Act to enforce higher wages by beginning the overtime sooner. Possibly the prohibition of overtime except in emergencies would meet the necessity of the case from the viewpoint of its advocates. However, I am taking a very hypothetical case at present, and perhaps there is no need of going further into what might be done if the committee took certain action.
As it turned out, the perhaps was fully justified. There was no need of going further as to what might be done, because the committee made no decision at all, and did not report any Bill last session. At this stage, however, the committee were very well satisfied with themselves. Perhaps I should have said the chairman rather than the committee, because the committee as a whole, do not speak here. However, there are some members other than the chairman who do speak. There is one member whom I used to know as a most enthusiastic advocate of the rights of labour in the part of Canada where I live. At one time he was simply a splendid fellow as a labour advocate. No trouble was too great for him to take, no distance was too far for him to go. So it was only natural on this occasion, when all this mass of evidence, so entirely favourable to the principle of shorter hours of labour had been presented, that the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Ralph Smith), should have been the first to express his appreciation of it. This is what I read on page 380:
Mr. Smith.-I desire to say, Mr. Chairman, that the splendid address which Professor Skelton has given ns this morning has been of the utmost assistance to the committee.
The Chairman.-Yes, indeed.
Mr. Smith.-His address to-day was simply
splendid, and I know from experience that his conclusions about England are absolutely correct. We can rely upon his address, and it will assist the committee very materially. _
The Chairman.-Professor Skelton, I think that the members of the committee are very much indebted to you for the thorough and systematic way in which you have investigated the legislation of the different countries on the subject of hours of labour, and given us the benefit of your researches.
Professor Skelton.-It is very good of you to say so. I have enjoyed my brief experience of parliamentary life behind the scenes. It has been indeed a great pleasure for me to assist in the committee's investigations.
Was all that printed at the expense of the country ?

Surely -a cord of it. Parliamenary life behind the scenes! Why, Mr. Speaker, he was not behind the scenes. He was only behind the first curtain. He had no idea of the operations which the scene shifters would set vigorously in motion the moment they got him off the premises. This recital would not be complete if we did not bring in the testimonial to Prof. Skelton, given by the father of the Bill:
Mr. Verville.-I must say that I consider Professor Skelton's report to be one of the best of the kind I ever heard in my life.
Although these explanations were the best which he, as an advocate of the cause of labour, had ever heard in his life, he asks us to adopt, not the magnificent programme which I have read to you, but something which he knows himself, is utterly meaningless, except as an affirmation of the principle, which has its sole value as an academic affirmation. Here is the valedictory of the chairman:
The Chairman.-I think you will see, Professor Skelton, that the members of tlie committee are unanimous in their appreciation of your work.
Now, it seems to -me that the Minister of Labour has another think coming, because I am satisfied that Prof. Skelton must now realize that the committee have no proper appreciation of his work, or, if they have, that these three gentlemen who heaped this deserved praise upon his last utterance there, would be standing up here vying with each other in urging upon the House that we too should show our appreciation of Prof. Skelton's services by enacting legislation which the experience of all other countries who have dealt with this subject shows to be wise legislation to adopt.
I am sorry to have taken up so much time, but I thought it due to myself, as a supporter of the Bill, to make some answer to the slighting remarks directed against me in my absence, impugning my conduct in common with that of other mem

bers on this side of the House as not being sincere. I think that, even at this late stage of the proceedings, we ought to have, from the Minister of Labour (Mr. King) some reason why he has thought fit to entirely ignore the recommendation of this professor who was called in by himself as an expert witness. When the hon. Minister of Labour and the hon. gentleman who has moved this Bill admitted that the conclusions of this professor were well founded and wise, and were a proper deduction from the experience of other countries, we ought to have some explanation why these conclusions and recommendations were dismissed so ignominiously as they were by the failure of both these hon. gentlemen to even refer to them in this House, and we ought to have some explanation why we are asked to read for a third time a Bill which falls so far short of the recommendations of that committee to which we referred the original measure.

I am sorry to say that I was away on the last two occasions when this Bill came up for discussion; and while I do not wish to detain the House at any length, I desire to take this opportunity of saying that I was in favour of the Bill as originally introduced. I have followed with very considerable interest, as a new member, the checkered career of this measure. I saw it on the Order Paper the first session I was here and found it quietly shelved; and I saw it again on the Order Paper last year and had a lesson in parliamentary juggling on the part of the government by referring it to an expert, whose opinion they evidently had not the slightest intention of following, and in this manner they succeeded in shelving it another year. My hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Taylor) has quoted the resolution of the Trades and Labour Council of the city of Victoria, in which they declare that the present mutilated measure is wholly ineffective and that the amendments introduced by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville) on compulsion-because I leave it to the judgment of any fair member of this House if those amendments were not the price given for the support of the government-utterly destroyed whatever merits the Bill in its original form possessed. I noticed an article in the Victoria ' Daily Times ' a few days ago to the effect that the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville), when this Bill was in committee, said that he was perfectly willing to withdraw his amendments, and that thereupon those members of the Conservative party, who said they supported the Bill in its original form, became immediately frightened and receded from the position they had taken.

I would like now to ask the Minister of Labour if he would allow the Bill to go through the House in its original Form, if the hon. member for Maisonneuve will withdraw his amendments? I have no reply but the answer is obvious. There was no doubt a bargain between the hon. . member for Maisonneuve and the government. The hon. gentleman took his Bill to the Minister of Labour (Mr. King), and I have not much doubt, although it does not appear in evidence, that the Minister of Labour drew up the amendments, and that the hon. member for Maisonneuve accepted them. I have nothing further to add except that I regret the Bill has been so mutilated and should be quite ready to support the measure as originally introduced.

I have listened with a good deal of interest to the discussion; and the question which has puzzled me is why there should be the discrimination we see in the Bill as it is now before the House. Why should the government allow a man working upon a government building have shorter hours of work than upon a canal or railway? Is one man not as good as the other? By this Bill, in its amended form, he is not. But if one man be as good as another, why not give the man working on the government canal or railway the same hours of labour as when working on a government building.
I have never yet heard a good reason why the Bill was amended. Has the originator of this Bill received any communications from the workingmen of Canada to the effect that they were not in favour of the Bill in its original form? If he has not, why has he attempted to amend it? Is there any opposition to the Bill? Why was the Bill not presented in its original form? I would like to ask the hon. gentleman to what extent does his amended Bill benefit the workingman? In its present shape would it benefit say 5 per cent of the workingmen of Canada? Would it benefit 2 per cent of our work-I ingmen, or even 1 per cent? I would like the hon. gentleman to answer that question.
If the Bill be accepted as it is and the principle adopted, probably my hon. friend will have reason to change his mind in five or six years.

That is not the answer I expected to get. I would like to ask the hon. gentleman still another question. As the hon. member has introduced this Bill in its present emasculated form, I would like to ask if he has received protests from any workingmen's organizations in Canada
Yes-from two cities out of the whole Dominion.
What cities?
Victoria and Vancouver.

My question to the hon. member who has introduced this Bill in its present emasculated form is : Has he received any protest from any of the labour organizations of Canada? If he has, why does he persist in bringing forward such a Bill in this House.
When the hon. member (Mr. Thoburn) has finished speaking, I will answer him if there is time. But I am not going to answer questions as he chooses to put them.

Will the Minister of Labour please answer that question? For, I can tell both these gentlemen that if they have not received such petitions, there are plenty of them in circulation. In addition to the petitions presented by the hon. member for New Westminster, I would like to present some that have been sent me from the labour organizations of the county I have the honour to represent and others, line first to Ibe called to my attention was the decision ibv the executive of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada in session in Montreal. The following is the account of the matter given in the public press :
That it cannot give fits approval to the proposed amendments in the eight-hour Bill to be introduced in parliament by Alphonse Verville, M.P., is the gist of a statement made public at 1.30 to-day by. the executive of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada after a session at the Windsor hotel last evening, which was attended by the Minister of Labour, and another this morning.
The statement is in part as follows:
'With reference to the eight-hour Bill and the proposed amendments now before parliament, the executive of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, after full and very serious consideration of the whole matter, has determined that it cannot give its approval to the" proposed amendments. Thh amendments, it is true, mean the recognition of the principle of the eight-hour day, but they are but a shadow of what the workers of this country are asking for. The proposed amendments give some benefit to the building trades, but will leave neglected most of those whom we represent. The principle of the eight-hour day has already been recognized by the government in numerous schedules enforced by it. That, , impliedly, is a recognition of the principle by parliament which has never protested or objected to those schedules.
'The executive feel that the proposed amendments do not fairly meet the enlightened sentiment of progressive Canada and are but a hesitating and faltering step towards the goal so generally sought in this country. Without further detail at the moment, the Trades and Labour Congress, through its executive, cannot, therefore, approve of the
proposed amendments and must stand by the Bill first introduced this session by Mr. Ver-ville.'
I have received a petition from the Trades and Labour Council of the county which I have the honour to represent which reads as follows :
Carleton Place, Ont., Jan. 30, 1911.
At a joint meeting of the trades unions held in Carleton Place on Thursday evening last, comprising representatives of the metal trades council, machinists, boilermakers, carmen, moulders, stove-mounters, polishers, blacksmiths and trackmen's locals, a committee was struck oft to draw up this letter to you defining our views on the eight-hour Bill and the amendments thereto.
We ask you as our representative to use your every effort to have Mr. Verville's Bill in it's original form. We consider that the manner in which this Bill has been mutilated by the Minister of Labour, who is supposed to be working in the interests of the workers of Canada, is a direct insult to us as a whole, and to Mr. Verville in particular as our representative labour member of parliament.
It appears to us as if the government wanted to get their caricature of a Bill through the House, in Mr. Verville's name, to be handed down as a specimen of labour legislature by a labour member.
Such legislation as the amended Bill promises to be is disgusting the workers here, and if there is a three-cornered fight at the next election we can thank the politicians who persist in ignoring the rights of the workers, who are beginning fast to realize they are the majority.
Committee, D. A. Bain, Wm. Simpson, John McPhail, George Humphrey.
(Sgd.) W. J. HAMMOND.
Will the hon. member say who drafted that communication?
It is drafted by the Trades and Labour Council of Carleton Place.
I understand that they passed it, but can the hon. gentleman say who wrote out the resolution?

The names of the committee appear upon the resolution as I have read it. Now, in the face of such evidence as this, I can only say that if the hon. member for Maisonnenve will introduce his original Bill, I shall have great pleasure in voting for it ; but I am bound to vote against the Bill in its present emasculated form.
